# HOW TO CONFIGURE CACHING

Click here for more info: https://www.drupal.org/docs/administering-a-drupal-site/internal-page-caching

To clear the cache run this:

```
$ drush cr
```

There are many ways to configure caching in Drupal. You can use Internal Page Cache, Dynamic Page Cache, BigPipe, Varnish, Redis, Memcache, or CDN modules. Each has different configuration steps.

You need to edit settings.php. Here is an example:

```
$ vim web/sites/default/settings.php
```

For Docker setup instructions see the Docker documentation. For installing PHP see the PHP manual. For setting up Apache see the Apache docs.

# Configure caching

Drupal ships with page caching enabled by default. Most sites need no
configuration at all — the work is usually *keeping* cached responses correct,
not turning caching on.

## TL;DR

Rebuild all caches after a code or configuration change:

```
drush cr
```

Check that the three core caching modules are installed, and set a browser and
proxy cache lifetime at **Administration › Configuration › Development ›
Performance** (`/admin/config/development/performance`).

That is the whole setup for a typical site. Everything below is for sites that
need more.

## Prerequisites

- A working Drupal site you can administer. Setting up a local environment is
  covered in [Configuring a local development environment](https://www.drupal.org/docs/develop/local-server-setup).
- The *Administer site configuration* permission, or user 1.
- [Drush](https://www.drush.org/) installed, for the command line steps.
- Write access to `sites/default/settings.php` if you plan to override cache
  backends.

## The three core caching layers

Drupal's standard profile installs all three. Leave them enabled in production.

- **[Internal Page Cache](https://www.drupal.org/docs/administering-a-drupal-site/internal-page-caching)**
  stores a complete rendered page for anonymous users and serves it without
  bootstrapping the rest of the request.
- **[Dynamic Page Cache](https://www.drupal.org/docs/administering-a-drupal-site/dynamic-page-cache)**
  caches pages for *all* users, including authenticated ones, leaving
  personalised sections as placeholders to be filled in per request.
- **[BigPipe](https://www.drupal.org/docs/core-modules-and-themes/core-modules/bigpipe-module)**
  streams those placeholders to the browser as they render, so the cached part
  of the page appears immediately.

If pages are serving stale or over-personalised content, the cause is almost
always missing or incorrect cache metadata on a render array or a block, not a
misconfigured module. Start with the
[Cache API documentation](https://www.drupal.org/docs/drupal-apis/cache-api) and
check the cache contexts, tags, and max-age on the code in question.

## Clearing caches

```
drush cr
```

This rebuilds every cache bin, including the container and the plugin,
discovery, and routing caches. It is the correct command after deploying code,
changing a `*.services.yml` file, or adding a new plugin.

To invalidate only what changed, use cache tags from code rather than a full
rebuild. Full rebuilds on a busy production site cause a thundering herd of
uncached requests.

## Overriding cache backends in settings.php

Only do this when you have a specific reason — an external cache backend, or
disabling caching locally.

Edit `sites/default/settings.php` (or better, a `settings.local.php` included
from it) and set the backend for a bin:

```php
$settings['cache']['bins']['render'] = 'cache.backend.null';
```

Never commit a null backend to production. Drupal core ships
`sites/example.settings.local.php` as a starting point for local overrides; copy
it to `sites/default/settings.local.php` and uncomment the include at the bottom
of `settings.php`. The full procedure is in
[Disable Drupal 8 caching during development](https://www.drupal.org/docs/develop/development-tools/disable-caching-and-enable-twig-debugging).

## Going beyond core

If core caching is correctly configured and the site is still slow, add an
external layer. In rough order of how often they are worth reaching for:

- **[Redis](https://www.drupal.org/project/redis)** or
  **[Memcache](https://www.drupal.org/project/memcache)** — move cache bins out
  of the database. Reach for this first when the `cache_*` tables are large or
  the database is the bottleneck.
- **[Varnish Purge](https://www.drupal.org/project/varnish_purge)** with
  **[Purge](https://www.drupal.org/project/purge)** — a reverse proxy in front
  of Drupal, with cache tag invalidation so pages expire when content changes.
- **A CDN**, driven by the same Purge module. Most hosting platforms provide
  one and document their own integration.

Pick one and configure it properly before adding another. Each additional layer
is another place for content to go stale.

## See also

- [Cache API](https://www.drupal.org/docs/drupal-apis/cache-api)
- [Caching in Drupal](https://www.drupal.org/docs/administering-a-drupal-site/caching)
- [Purge module documentation](https://www.drupal.org/docs/contributed-modules/purge)
